CHARGING ORDER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Holdings, LLC

CHARGING ORDER INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Holdings, LLC, a limited liability company formed under the law of California, and to Jordan Lee, a member (or transferee of a member's interest) of Acme Holdings, LLC. It describes California Corporations Code § 17705.03, part of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, which governs the remedy available to a judgment creditor of an LLC member or transferee against that person's transferable interest in the LLC — as distinct from any remedy against the LLC's own assets, and as distinct from this corpus's LLC Operating Agreement and LLC Dissolution and Cancellation documents, which address the LLC's own internal governance and winding up rather than a third party's remedy against an individual member's interest. This information sheet does not determine whether any judgment has been or will be entered against Jordan Lee, does not determine whether any specific creditor is entitled to a charging order or any further relief under § 17705.03, and does not evaluate any specific creditor's, member's, or transferee's rights or exposure under any specific set of facts. Whether a charging order should issue, and what further relief a court should order, are determinations made by a court applying § 17705.03 to the facts and evidence presented in that proceeding.

WHAT A CHARGING ORDER IS AND DOES
Under California law, a judgment creditor of an LLC member or of a transferee of a member's interest may apply to a court for a charging order against that person's transferable interest in the LLC, for the unsatisfied amount of the judgment. A charging order operates in two ways at once: it constitutes a lien on the judgment debtor's transferable interest in the LLC, and it requires the LLC itself to pay over to the person the charging order was issued to any distribution that would otherwise be paid to the judgment debtor. The charging order therefore reaches only the judgment debtor's right to receive distributions and other economic rights that make up the transferable interest — the statute does not, by its own terms, transfer membership status, voting rights, or management rights to the judgment creditor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "On application by a judgment creditor of a member or transferee, a court may enter a charging order against the transferable interest of the judgment debtor for the unsatisfied amount of the judgment. A charging order constitutes a lien on a judgment debtor’s transferable interest and requires the limited liability company to pay over to the person to which the charging order was issued any distribution that would otherwise be paid to the judgment debtor."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, charging order against a member's or transferee's interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17705.03.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn entirely from California Corporations Code § 17705.03(a). It states only what a charging order is and what it directly requires (a lien plus a pay-over obligation on the LLC); it does not address separately, from any other statute, what rights a transferee (as opposed to the original member) otherwise holds, since that is addressed by a different section (§ 17705.02) that this document does not independently verify or cover here.

THE CHARGING ORDER IS THE EXCLUSIVE REMEDY AGAINST A MEMBER'S INTEREST
California's LLC statute states directly that the charging order procedure is the exclusive remedy by which a person seeking to enforce a judgment against a member or transferee may, acting as judgment creditor, satisfy the judgment out of the judgment debtor's transferable interest in the LLC. This exclusivity language governs remedies against the member's or transferee's transferable interest specifically — it does not, by its own terms, address or limit a creditor's remedies against assets that belong to the LLC itself rather than to the individual member, which is a different question from the one § 17705.03 answers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This section provides the exclusive remedy by which a person seeking to enforce a judgment against a member or transferee may, in the capacity of judgment creditor, satisfy the judgment from the judgment debtor’s transferable interest."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, exclusive remedy against a transferable interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17705.03.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes California Corporations Code § 17705.03(f) directly and states only what that subdivision itself says. This document does not address, and takes no position on, whether or how a creditor might separately reach LLC-owned assets directly (for example, through a judgment against the LLC itself), since that is outside the scope of what § 17705.03 governs and was not independently researched here.

WHAT A COURT MAY ADDITIONALLY ORDER, INCLUDING FORECLOSURE
Beyond entering the charging order itself, the statute lists specific further steps a court may take, to the extent necessary to effectuate collection of distributions under a charging order already in effect: the court may appoint a receiver of the distributions subject to the charging order, with the power to make all inquiries the judgment debtor might have made, and the court may make all other orders necessary to give effect to the charging order. The statute also authorizes foreclosure specifically, but only upon a particular showing: if it is shown that distributions under the charging order will not pay the judgment debt within a reasonable time, the court may foreclose the lien and order the sale of the transferable interest. Even then, a purchaser at that foreclosure sale acquires only the transferable interest itself — the purchaser does not thereby become a member of the LLC, and the purchaser's rights are governed by the separate statute addressing transferees' rights generally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "To the extent necessary to effectuate the collection of distributions pursuant to a charging order in effect under subdivision (a), the court may do any of the following: (1) Appoint a receiver of the distributions subject to the charging order, with the power to make all inquiries the judgment debtor might have made. (2) Make all other orders necessary to give effect to the charging order. (3) Upon a showing that distributions under a charging order will not pay the judgment debt within a reasonable time, foreclose the lien and order the sale of the transferable interest. The purchaser at the foreclosure sale obtains only the transferable interest, does not thereby become a member, and is subject to Section 17705.02."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, further court orders and conditioned foreclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17705.03.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn entirely from California Corporations Code § 17705.03(b), a single subdivision with three numbered paragraphs (receiver appointment, other necessary orders, and conditioned foreclosure), reproduced together here because all three describe the same category of relief (further court orders to effectuate an existing charging order) and the third expressly conditions foreclosure on a showing not required for the first two. This document does not evaluate, for any specific case, whether distributions would or would not pay a judgment debt within a reasonable time, or whether a court would exercise its discretion to appoint a receiver or order foreclosure on any particular facts. Paragraph (b)(3)'s cross-reference to Section 17705.02 (governing a transferee's rights generally) was not independently verified against that section's own text and is stated here only as the cross-reference § 17705.03 itself makes, not as an independent characterization of what Section 17705.02 provides.

EXTINGUISHING THE CHARGING ORDER AND THE LLC'S OR OTHER MEMBERS' REDEMPTION RIGHT
The statute gives two distinct paths to end a charging order before any foreclosure sale takes place. First, at any time before foreclosure, the member or transferee whose transferable interest is subject to the charging order may extinguish it by satisfying the judgment and filing a certified copy of the satisfaction with the court that issued the charging order. Second, and separately, at any time before foreclosure, the LLC itself, or one or more members whose transferable interests are not subject to the charging order, may pay the judgment creditor the full amount due under the judgment; doing so lets the LLC or those members succeed to the rights of the judgment creditor, including the charging order itself. The statute does not require the LLC or any other member to make this payment — it authorizes them to do so, at their option, as a way of controlling who holds the charging order against the debtor-member's interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "At any time before foreclosure under paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), the member or transferee whose transferable interest is subject to a charging order under subdivision (a) may extinguish the charging order by satisfying the judgment and filing a certified copy of the satisfaction with the court that issued the charging order."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, extinguishing a charging order by satisfying the judgment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17705.03.)
  "At any time before foreclosure under paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), a limited liability company or one or more members whose transferable interests are not subject to the charging order may pay to the judgment creditor the full amount due under the judgment and thereby succeed to the rights of the judgment creditor, including the charging order."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, LLC or other members' right to pay the judgment and succeed to the creditor's rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17705.03.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two adjacent subdivisions of the same statutory section, California Corporations Code § 17705.03(c) (the debtor-member's own extinguishment right) and § 17705.03(d) (the LLC's or other members' optional redemption right) — not independently sourced provisions, but two related mechanisms within the same section reproduced together because both operate on the same "before foreclosure" timing and both terminate the charging order in the debtor-member's favor. This document does not evaluate whether the LLC named in this information sheet or any specific member would choose to exercise the redemption right described here, and does not state that any such payment is required.

EXEMPTION LAWS ARE PRESERVED — THE STATUTE DOES NOT ITSELF COMPEL A DISTRIBUTION
The statute expressly preserves any exemption laws that would otherwise apply to a member's or transferee's transferable interest: the LLC statute governing charging orders does not deprive any member or transferee of the benefit of any exemption laws applicable to that person's transferable interest. Separately, the mechanics described elsewhere in this statute show that a charging order operates by redirecting distributions the LLC decides to make, and by lien and (where the statutory showing is met) foreclosure of the interest itself — the statute's own text does not say that a charging order, by itself, forces the LLC or its other members to declare or make a distribution that the LLC would not otherwise have made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This title does not deprive any member or transferee of the benefit of any exemption laws applicable to the member’s or transferee’s transferable interest."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, preservation of exemption laws (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17705.03.)
  Known gap: The exemption-law preservation is drawn directly from California Corporations Code § 17705.03(e). The second sentence of this clause is not a separate statutory quotation; it is this document's own observation, based on the absence of any compel-a-distribution language anywhere in the verified text of § 17705.03(a) through (f), that the section's mechanism (lien plus pay-over-if-distributed, or foreclosure on the stated showing) is what the statute provides, rather than a power to force a distribution — this document does not cite a separate statute or case establishing that no other law could compel a distribution, and takes no position on whether some other statute, the LLC's operating agreement, or common-law fiduciary duties might independently bear on if or when distributions must be made.
